items.u:
The Information recently reported that Nvidia has put $170 billion on the line to support neoclouds. But we found that the company’s overall committed capital extends much further. Tallying the disclosures in Nvidia’s latest 10-Q reveals a whopping $530.5 billion in future commitments and guarantees. 

The obligations span several buckets: supply commitments, equity injections into neoclouds, backstop guarantees for data centers, and agreements to purchase unused capacity from partners. 

The $530.5 billion figure doesn’t include deals that post-date the 10-Q, like the preliminary agreement Nvidia just reached to inject $100 billion of equity in 10 installments into OpenAI, each one tied to OpenAI placing orders for Nvidia chips, or any of those European deals. 

Taken together, the numbers show how much Nvidia is putting on the line to keep the flywheel turning. “Is Nvidia now the central bank and lender of last resort?” asked the longtime investor Doug Kass of Seabreeze Partners Management in a recent column. “Is the Federal Reserve’s Kevin Warsh the boss, or is it now Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?” 

Perhaps the bigger question, to switch the metaphor, is what will happen if the arsonist feeding the flames also has to put out the fire?

The Commitments Behind the Boom

“Circularity” — the idea that Nvidia invests money in a company that then buys its chips — doesn’t do justice to the reality. The company is making advance commitments for parts it needs so that it can secure supply. It is signing leases on data centers for its own work and also guaranteeing the leases on data centers for other companies in the event they can’t pay. It invests in neoclouds that buy its GPUs, yes, but may also have money in the customers of these neoclouds, like frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI.

It's one thing to grease the skids. It’s another thing if companies and data centers and investment coalitions that wouldn’t otherwise get financed do so only because of Nvidia’s involvement. In other words, the company could be increasing the risk in the overall system. And if the cracks continue to grow, the worry is that not even Nvidia’s dollars would be able to paper them over. 

Nvidia has started to disclose more of its commitments, in part to address investors’ worries about the scale of its exposure. And the way Nvidia thinks about its own numbers is revealing. The baseline category, which it labels “future commitments,” stood at $366 billion as of July 26. The figure’s largest component is $279 billion in advance purchase orders and pledges to various suppliers of memory and of the packaging, testing, substrate and optical components Nvidia needs for its systems. Nvidia’s CFO said at the end of the first quarter that high bandwidth memory chips the company depends on primarily accounted for the surge. 

This line item is getting bigger fast — the $279 billion was up from just $119 billion three months earlier, which is an increase of $160 billion or 134%.

Since the end of the second quarter, it has gotten even bigger. On October 21, Nvidia announced an expansion of its commitments with six suppliers. A big one is Siliconware Precision Industries, a Taiwanese semiconductor packaging and testing company. Nvidia said SPIL aims to increase capacity for optical engines used in co-packaged optics 15-fold by mid-2027. Nvidia didn’t put a dollar amount on the commitment. 

Theoretically, locking in supply before others do is an advantage. Throughout 2025 and 2026, Huang himself criscrossed Asia, securing deals. Bulls see this as one of the smartest things that Nvidia has done. One reason Google’s competing TPUs may not have scaled as quickly is because of supply shortages. 

Nvidia doesn't name its suppliers or disclose deal-by-deal terms. It says some agreements “may be cancelable, rescheduled, or adjustable” before firm orders are placed, but doesn't say what share is firm. If demand for Nvidia’s chips doesn’t grow as it expects, then of course it loses the anticipated revenue, but may also find itself on the hook to pay its suppliers. 

This is the financial trap fiber optic companies like Lucent and Nortel found themselves in after the dot-com bubble burst. They were each stuck with over $1 billion — which was real money back then — in charges for suppliers and inventory that the market no longer wanted. Compared to Nvidia’s current balance sheet commitments, those figures look positively quaint. In 2000, Cisco, which also had massive exposure to vendor financing, seemed to have everything under control. “They knew exactly what was going to happen — until they didn’t,” says Fitzgerald. 

Cisco’s stock price only returned to its 2000 high last year, in December. 

Another part of the $366 billion ledger is $29 billion in something called “cloud service agreements,” which is money Nvidia is committed to pay for internal research. In February, an Indian company called Yotta announced that it was hosting capacity for Nvidia's DGX Cloud service in a four-year agreement that it said was worth more than $1 billion. 

Yotta is simultaneously a major buyer of Nvidia’s chips. So in effect, Nvidia sells Yotta the equipment, and then becomes a customer for some of the cloud capacity that Yotta builds with it. Yotta says that Nvidia is expected to account for roughly half of the outtake, meaning that Yotta’s operating model is heavily dependent on its anchor vendor, Nvidia. 

Another $25 billion of the $366 billion is for leases that Nvidia has on data centers for its internal engineering facilities. Nvidia doesn’t name the sites or landlords. There’s also $25 billion in pending equity commitments, a portion of which could reflect Nvidia’s $30 billion investment in OpenAI, which has not been completely funded yet. 

The last tranche of the $366 billion is another $8 billion in capital expenditures, mainly for data-center infrastructure and testing equipment for internal operations. The filing doesn’t name a specific project.

The Circle Game

Beyond that $366 billion, Nvidia reported another $56 billion that it labeled “additional commitments.” This one consists of $36 billion in AI-cloud agreements (in which Nvidia commits to buy cloud capacity from neoclouds that bought its hardware; the neoclouds can pull that capacity back and sell it to other customers, which shrinks Nvidia's obligation) and $20 billion in data-center leases that have not yet begun and which Nvidia plans to reassign to third parties. The second quarter was the first in which Nvidia’s 10-Q broke all these figures out into a dedicated reporting category, so the historical run rate can’t be tracked. 

CoreWeave illustrates how the mechanics work. In 2025, it disclosed a $6.3 billion order that obligates Nvidia to buy residual capacity CoreWeave can’t sell to other customers through April 2032. 

Nvidia is also an investor in CoreWeave. At the start of 2026, Nvidia invested $2 billion in CoreWeave. OpenAI, another investee, also buys CoreWeave compute. To close the loop, OpenAI invested directly in CoreWeave. 

The relationships can be mutually beneficial when business is booming. It helps Nvidia set up its own ecosystem in the event that the hyperscalers turn to competing chips. And it’s likely that Nvidia has some kind of revenue sharing agreement, meaning it will participate in the upside beyond the value of its equity. But if demand slows, the financing loop can be problematic. If a major customer cuts its spending with CoreWeave, that could not only hurt the value of Nvidia’s investment but also increase the amount of unused capacity Nvidia would have to buy, subject to the terms of the agreement.

Other arrangements Nvidia has are less clear. In June, SharonAI ($SHAZ), an Australian neocloud provider, announced a six-year compute collaboration with Nvidia, with a stated contract value of up to $4.88 billion. SharonAI’s filing says that it may try to sell the compute to third parties and split the revenues with Nvidia. The filing doesn’t illuminate the details further. 

As for the $20 billion in data center leases, it looks like Nvidia signs those upfront and plans to subsequently transfer them to neocloud counterparties. Nvidia describes these leases as roughly 15-year commitments, which are expected to start in fiscal 2028 or 2029 and then be reassigned to third parties. It isn't clear if that's supposed to happen before or after the construction is complete.

Consider the data centers that Miami-based Hut 8 ($HUT) — which itself posts huge losses — is building at Beacon Point in Texas. The Financial Times identified Nvidia as the tenant. But the Wall Street Journal reported that Lambda, a privately held cloud computing company backed by Nvidia, has a $35 billion deal to provide computing to Anthropic at the facility. Nvidia will provide the chips. The deal, as the Journal noted, helps Lambda get a contract with Anthropic without needing to lease a data center on its own. 

The terms under which Nvidia would share any of Lambda’s revenues aren’t disclosed. 

In effect, Nvidia is no longer a chip supplier but rather a credit backstop for data center developers. 

What Happens If a Tenant Can’t Pay?

Layered on top of that $366 billion is another $108.5 billion, which represents a different way in which Nvidia is supporting data centers. In this case, Nvidia isn’t the tenant. Instead, Nvidia has agreed to cover the shortfall if the tenant defaults. 

By far the deal’s largest component — accounting for $105 billion — is tied to SB Energy, a SoftBank portfolio company, and its massive PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio, built for OpenAI. In essence, if OpenAI cannot pay, Nvidia is on the hook for up to $105 billion. Nvidia also has agreed to make a $3 billion investment in SB Energy.

SB Energy was supposed to go public this fall, but postponed its IPO amid pushback about the valuation it wanted and broader questions about data centers. Investors also questioned SB Energy’s reliance on OpenAI. Indeed, what’s striking about this is that OpenAI’s commitment reportedly wasn’t enough. The deal needed Nvidia’s backstop. 

That shows the doubt that is increasingly creeping into the ecosystem, and how all roads lead back to Nvidia. If Nvidia is using its credibility to bridge what will turn out to be short-lived shakiness, it’s a smart move. It’ll seem less smart if the temporary wobble turns into a bigger rout. 

In a fun additional bit of circularity showing Nvidia isn’t the only one doing it: The tenant at one of SB Energy’s first data center projects, dubbed Cosmos, in Austin, Texas, is an affiliate of SoftBank. SB Energy expects approximately $2.5 billion in rent over the next 15 years.

The data and R&D center will be occupied by Graphcore, an AI chipmaker SoftBank purchased in 2024. Graphcore itself had no product sales revenue as of its latest annual filing for the period ending in March 2025, relying almost entirely on SoftBank for R&D funding.

Nvidia the Investor

Another way to think about Nvidia’s commitments is through an entirely separate category, its equity investments. These create loops that aren’t so much circular as they are reflexive and self-reinforcing — at least, until they are not. 

Nvidia has equity stakes in the companies it’s doing these deals with. In total, the company has $99 billion in equity investments, which it makes both through its venture capital arm, NVentures, and at the corporate level. The portfolio spans 229 private companies and 13 publicly traded companies. According to a recent 13F SEC filing, the investments include Intel ($INTC), SpaceX ($SPCX), CoreWeave, Coherent ($COHR), Nokia ($NOK), Nebius ($NBIS) and more; across the public and private portfolio, the investments range from data center construction and AI model development to energy supply and hardware manufacturing. 

Nvidia’s second-biggest publicly traded stake — behind Intel — is in SpaceX. It owns 122.8 million SpaceX shares, which it acquired by helping to fund xAI, which SpaceX later bought. The stake is worth roughly $17 billion today. On the company’s first earnings call, Musk announced that SpaceX was “exclusive to Nvidia.” SpaceX just raised $40 billion in debt, a large portion of which is earmarked for the purchase of Nvidia’s chips. 

The figure also includes Nvidia’s funded investments in OpenAI and Anthropic. The publicly held securities are marked to market quarterly, but the private ones are held at cost and written up when a new funding round sets a higher price. 

In the first half of fiscal 2027, Nvidia recorded $23.7 billion in net equity gains, representing almost 17% of pretax income. A downward turn in valuations would of course cut the other way. 

While the portfolio looks diversified, it is in reality a concentrated bet on AI. And the companies are usually buyers of Nvidia’s chips. For instance, in October 2024, Poolside, an AI model and software company, announced that it had brought 10,000 Nvidia GPUs online; Nvidia has also helped to fund Poolside. So Nvidia is both an investor and supplier. As is often the case, the size of its investment and the share returned through sales of chips to Poolside aren’t disclosed. So long as Poolside succeeds, Nvidia prospers, but if it fails, Nvidia suffers in two ways: Its equity investment loses money, and its sales to Poolside go away. 

The more you dig into it, the more elaborate the relationships are. Nvidia-backed companies may buy chips from Nvidia, but they may also buy computing from neoclouds that Nvidia backs. For instance, Nvidia has invested in AI software companies Mistral and Cohere, both of which use Nvidia’s chips. Both companies also use CoreWeave for compute capacity. So if Mistral or Cohere were to fail, that would hurt Nvidia’s investment and chip sales. But it would also take customers away from CoreWeave, which might put Nvidia on the hook to buy CoreWeave’s capacity, as well as negatively impact the value of the stake Nvidia has in CoreWeave. 

All three companies — Poolside, Mistral and Cohere — are private, so it’s difficult to know if they are profitable or not. But assuming they are still dependent on venture capital, that means their health depends on the willingness of investors to continue funding them.

Nvidia’s investments can be hard to track, in part because Nvidia is also investing in the funds that themselves make investments in AI. For instance, Brookfield, the investment manager, identified Nvidia as the $2 billion anchor limited partner in its AI infrastructure fund. It isn’t fully clear what investments that fund has made, or what share Nvidia has of them. 

Brookfield also says that Nvidia is a critical supplier to at least one portfolio company. 

Separately, Nvidia is also investing $1 billion in a Korean internet company called NAVER whose data center buildout is being partly financed by Brookfield; NAVER is buying Nvidia’s chips. Brookfield’s September Investor Day transcript does not disclose how much of Nvidia’s commitment has been funded or its share of each underlying asset. 

Brookfield is also one of the six firms in Nvidia’s announced compute-financing initiative, alongside Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The group aims to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital for Nvidia-based AI infrastructure. The arrangement is yet another way for Nvidia to make sure that customers can afford to buy its chips without necessarily financing the purchases themselves. One way to read this is an attempt on Nvidia’s part to have other deep-pocketed investors help pay for the Nvidia-based infrastructure that AI companies need. The key question is how much risk outside investors are willing to take, and how much risk Nvidia will have to retain in order to persuade them to participate. Huang said on X that Nvidia could backstop up to $125 billion, or 25%, of the deals. (The initiative is similar to Broadcom’s financing arrangement with Anthropic, which uses Alphabet’s TPUs, in that both aim to help customers access computing capacity while encouraging reliance on a particular chip supplier.)

Nvidia’s relationship with British AI company Nscale provides another example of its overlapping roles. Nvidia has committed $1 billion in convertible loan notes to the company, in which it also apparently has a stake. At Nscale’s Ward County, Texas facility, Nvidia guarantees up to $860.3 million of rent for the first five lease years. The Information recently reported that Nvidia is in talks to potentially provide more than $5 billion in guarantees for another data center Nscale is building (with Nvidia chips, of course) in West Virginia; if Nscale were to default, Nvidia would step in, even though Anthropic has a $45 billion contract with Nscale for this facility. 

Nscale’s S-1 filing also lists $24 billion of outstanding commitments to buy equipment for 2026 and 2027; it isn’t clear how much of this is purchases from Nvidia. 

Nscale has had to delay its IPO amid investor skepticism. Firmus, the Australian data center firm that has a similar arrangement with in which Nvidia, has had to pull its public listing. The Information has reported that after Firmus’s IPO was pulled, Nvidia and Firmus began discussions for Nvidia to inject several hundred million dollars into it.

The talks could demonstrate Nvidia’s ability to cover a funding gap. Alternatively, they could leave Nvidia with more money invested in companies that outside investors are unwilling to finance.

What Happens When the Carousel Halts?

So is Huang right when he says that for every $1 Nvidia invests, $100 is coming back? Unfortunately, there is no way to independently verify that. Nor is it possible to estimate what share of Nvidia’s revenue is dependent on demand that it is funding or protecting. 

Unsurprisingly, Nvidia says its exposure is manageable. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress said on the August earnings call that Nvidia’s “risk is limited” in backing AI labs because it can redeploy its chips to other customers. Nvidia did not return several requests for comment and clarification.

But that’s true only as long as any problems remain isolated, rather than part of a more systemic breakdown. 

Ramp economist Ara Kharazian says that 80% of spend on OpenAI and Anthropic is driven by 1% of firms. In an interview with Derek Thompson, Kharazian pointed out that these customers are heavily concentrated in software and technology. It isn’t clear to what extent these customers are being financed by venture capital, or to what extent apparent demand for AI might be demand created by investors betting on AI — and supposedly disparate demand might all be correlated. If those customers need a continued influx of funds to keep spending, then any downturn could cause a lot of demand to evaporate. 

On top of that, research firm Gartner has predicted that by 2030, 80% of neoclouds will cease independent operations. And the need for more and more capital means that the boom is in the hands of an increasingly wary — and expensive — bond market.

The hedge fund Orso also warns there may be a massive oversupply of compute, which could be a huge problem for the circular GPU economy. Greener points out that there was a dress rehearsal for this very scenario. In 2017 and 2018, demand for Nvidia chips was skyrocketing, because cryptocurrency miners were grabbing them to mine Ethereum. When that market crashed, demand evaporated, and Nvidia chips reportedly ended up on eBay for resale.

Any one of these scenarios could trigger losses for Nvidia. If neoclouds default, Nvidia loses the chip sales and its investments and is on the hook for some amount of rent payments. If venture capital backed AI companies that are in the top 1% cut back on their AI spending, that harms Nvidia’s investments and chip sales. If demand for its products declines, Nvidia is on the hook for supply commitments it may no longer need. If OpenAI or Anthropic cannot pull off their IPOs, then Nvidia’s investments in those companies are worth less, and they have to raise additional money from the private market in order to make good on their commitments. (OpenAI reportedly has raised less than half the $30 billion it had initially targeted for its latest funding round.) That in turn would likely increase both the draw from Nvidia as an investor and the likelihood that Nvidia will be liable for the various rent guarantees. 

And on and on. Each of these is manageable in isolation, and Fitzgerald points out that Nvidia’s fat margins mean that it could still emerge as a highly profitable company in many scenarios. But then again, what looks like linear logic can become chaos theory once the music stops. Or to put it differently, when fear sets in, the outcome stops being predictable. 

That said, Nvidia generates massive amounts of cash. From the beginning of fiscal 2027, through the end of fiscal 2028, the company is expected to produce over $500 billion in free cash flow. With that, plus its cash on hand, the company could cover all of its commitments. (And even in a worst-case scenario, those commitments don’t come due right away.) But of course, the commitments are getting bigger rapidly, and some of Nvidia’s money is spoken for. 

In the first half of fiscal 2027, the company generated about $70 billion of free cash flow and spent a net $35 billion on investments. If Nvidia’s growth in chip revenues is dependent on its continued investments, then those investment dollars aren’t discretionary. On top of that, Nvidia has authorized a remaining $235 billion to a massive share buyback. If it were to rescind that, its stock would likely fall. 

And if Nvidia were to falter, the market would likely crash. Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to report a 30% rise in third-quarter earnings from a year ago, but just two companies — Nvidia and Micron — are projected to account for 34% of that growth. Bulls point out that after its 15% slide from its high in early October, Nvidia’s stock is selling for less than 15 times fiscal 2028’s estimated earnings. After the massacre on November 5, the stock arguably is even cheaper.

Whether this is a buying opportunity or a harbinger of problems to come depends on the answer to the great question of our day: Whither the AI boom?

Engage your harness. The vertical loop on this one could be stomach-churning.

items.t: What Lies Beneath: The Developer Building a Data Center on a Former Army Dump Laced With Munitions and Carcinogens
items.u:
In 2025, Digital Realty spent $120 million to purchase a 97-acre parcel of land that was once part of Fort Gillem, a former United States Army post in Forest Park, Georgia. The company, one of the world’s largest real estate investment trusts, is constructing a massive data center complex on the site, returning valuable land to a “productive, tax-generating use,” as its executives put it.

But the land came with a historical burden. From 1941 until around 1980 the Army dumped everything from gas masks and medical waste to solvents and sewage sludge on this parcel in the northwest corner of the former army base that now houses a maze of warehouses, including a Kroger distribution center and an Amazon delivery station. 

There’s quite a bit of environmental issues with the site,” a Digital Realty asset manager said at a meeting with county officials in 2025. “Tons and tons and tons of — physical tons — of trash and environmental hazards.”

An investigation by Hunterbrook found that the hazards unearthed included military waste that was still combustible. Meanwhile, residents in neighboring communities are reporting cracks on their walls from explosive blasting on the site and say their questions about environmental and health threats stemming from Digital Realty’s Fort Gillem project are being ignored. 

The company plans to spend $3 billion on this project, and the first phase is expected to open in early 2028. But a document filed with the Georgia Environmental Protection Division suggests construction may surface some surprises.

In December 2025, the company encountered white phosphorus on the property, which “reacted when exposed to air and exhibited a dense white smoke,” according to a letter an environmental consultant sent on behalf of Digital Realty to Georgia EPD. The company asked the Army for guidance and contacted the local police department, which sent a bomb squad to inspect and sample the material.

The letter states that the white phosphorus was found in an area on the western side of the property that’s going to be under the planned data center.

“Upon completion of the Property’s redevelopment, the area of concern will be encapsulated with a concrete building foundation,” the letter states. “At this time, the size of the area of concern is not known but is not anticipated to be larger than 100-feet by 100-feet by 8-feet deep based on grading already completed at the Property.” 

The material has since been removed, a Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook in an email.

“Trained professionals carefully excavated the 100-foot by 100-foot by 8-foot area in accordance with an approved work plan, using appropriate equipment and personal protective equipment to identify any additional material containing white phosphorus,” the spokesperson wrote. “The excavation recovered five 30-gallon steel drums of material containing white phosphorus, far less than could have been encountered across the full area. The drums were then transported under a hazardous waste manifest to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility.”

The company also said that “work in the area where the material was initially discovered was stopped immediately upon the discovery of the material” and that “there were no reported injuries.” No other munitions and explosives of concern have been encountered since the white phosphorus discovery, according to Digital Realty. 

A Georgia EPD spokesperson confirmed the temporary work stoppage in the area where white phosphorus was found and that Digital Realty was in the process of removing the material in February, when EPD representatives visited the site. 

White phosphorus is used in artillery shells, rockets, and grenades to create dense smoke screens, provide battlefield illumination, mark targets, or act as an incendiary weapon. The use of white phosphorus weapons in civilian areas has been considered a war crime by human rights organizations like Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International. Its presence at the Digital Realty construction site “is assumed to be associated with historical Army disposal operations,” according to the letter to the Georgia EPD.

“Measures are in place to protect construction workers, future occupants, and the public throughout remediation and development activities,” the Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook.

Toxic Land Is Data Center Boom’s Next Frontier

The frenzied AI build-out has turned Digital Realty into a digital infrastructure colossus. According to its website, Digital Realty operates more than 300 data centers worldwide. It counts Oracle, IBM, Meta, AT&T, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Morgan Stanley among its customers. 

Amid the scramble to feed AI’s seemingly endless need for compute, other companies besides Digital Realty have resorted to building data centers on contaminated land. TeraWulf is developing the former Century Aluminum smelter site in Hawesville, Kentucky, into a more than $4 billion data center campus, with Anthropic as its tenant. Decades of smelter waste disposal and PCB spills left both soil and groundwater at this site contaminated.

SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, is building a campus of up to 10 gigawatts (roughly eight of which OpenAI has contracted) on land that also includes the former Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant in Pike County, Ohio, which enriched uranium between 1954 and 2001. Operations at the plant generated hazardous and radioactive waste and "resulted in soil and groundwater contamination at areas located within plant boundaries," according to the Department of Energy.
‍
And Sentinel Data Centers has begun building a project at the Foote Mineral Co. Superfund site in East Whiteland Township, Pennsylvania, where lithium metal and chemical production contaminated the soil with arsenic and hexavalent chromium.

Concerns over possible health impacts caused East Whiteland Township to order Sentinel Data Centers and its development partner Green Fig LLC to stop work on their data center in early July until “greater clarity is provided with respect to the ongoing review of the Soils Management Plan (SMP) and Health & Safety Plan (HSP) by the Township,” according to an announcement on Facebook. Residents had told the Philadelphia Inquirer that they had seen “dust plumes rising from the site” in June. Work at the construction site resumed later in July, according to the Inquirer, though work was partially halted again in late August over questions regarding the data center’s water supply.

Construction on Digital Realty’s campus, by contrast, continues apace.

Digital Realty has acknowledged that the land it bought comes with a considerable environmental cleanup burden. After all, the Army base’s toxic legacy was no secret: In 2000, workers discovered a burn pit with ash at astronomical lead levels of up to 25,000 milligrams per kilogram. In 2009, they unearthed rusted drums labeled "Trichloroethylene Tech" (TCE is a known carcinogen that is linked to kidney cancer.) And a chemical-warfare-clothing compound called “XXCC3” had also been detected in the soil here. 

Urban Redevelopment Agency (URA) chair Kimberly James told Hunterbrook in an email that “Digital Realty is undertaking substantial environmental remediation efforts and site work” — efforts that Digital Realty has put more than a $100 million tag on.

“We expect to invest more than $100 million in site remediation and environmental work, including stream mitigation, methane remediation, and soil and bedrock stabilization,” the company’s website for the project states. 

Digital Realty’s most recent annual filing lists environmental contamination as a general business risk, without naming the Fort Gillem project specifically. 
‍
“The presence of contamination or the failure to remediate contamination at our properties may expose us to third-party liability or materially adversely affect our ability to sell, lease or develop the real estate or to borrow using the real estate as collateral,” Digital Realty’s risk disclosures read.  

Fort Gillem’s toxic footprint is massive. The Army buried chlorinated solvents, including the known carcinogen TCE, and household trash that now generates methane.

Groundwater plumes containing solvents have migrated beyond the fence line and reached residential wells. After toxic vapors were found seeping into nearby homes in 2014, the Army installed a ventilation system beneath a nearby daycare and agreed to place carbon air filters in 22 homes, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. 

The future data centers in Forest Park may face the same risk of soil vapor intrusion into buildings, which is why the environmental consultant in a letter to the Georgia Environmental Protection Division (EPD) said that a mitigation system "designed to address both chlorinated volatile organic compounds (CVOCs) and landfill gas (e.g., methane)" will be installed.

“Onsite data center buildings will be constructed with vapor mitigation systems to protect against chlorinated volatile organic compounds. To the extent warranted based on sampling data and advice from qualified environmental professionals, methane-specific components will also be included in the mitigation systems,” the Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook. “All decisions related to onsite data center buildings are based on current, onsite data, not from historic offsite data related to neighboring properties.”

And noxious fumes are not the only hazards facing construction workers and future employees. The Army’s 2023 property transfer report also warns of buried expended ordnance, spent munitions that had already been fired. But there’s always a risk of happening upon munitions that didn’t detonate, and the Army requires anyone who finds suspected unexploded munitions to immediately stop work and call the police department. That’s exactly what happened after workers discovered the aforementioned white phosphorus, which turned out to be still combustible.

For nearby residents, the explosive remnants of war are just one of many concerns linked to the Digital Realty construction site, which has literally been rattling their lives.

Residents Say Blasting Caused Cracks in Walls, Seek Transparency

Pamela Felder, who said she bought her “forever” home less than a mile from the Digital Realty project three years ago, says blasting at the construction site earlier this year has damaged her home.

Blasting is the controlled use of explosives to break up and remove hard rock and dense soil for excavation and site preparation.

The blasting, which Felder said felt like somebody picked her home up and dropped it back down, has left numerous cracks inside and outside her and her neighbors' homes, she said.

Documents obtained by Forest Park resident Zack Parker through Georgia Open Records Act requests and shared with Hunterbrook include a contractor's schedule for 67 days of rock blasting at the data center site's substation and building pads, from early December 2025 through late February, plus 38 additional days listed as "overblast." 

After Felder complained to the blasting company, Maine Drilling & Blasting, an inspector sent out by the company diagnosed the cracks as “settling,” Felder said. She tried to claim damages through a prepaid legal service, but “they denied me a second time,” she said.

Felder is unsure what her options are. She said it would cost $5,000 to retain a lawyer, “which was out of my budget.”

“Blasting-related damages claims were thoroughly evaluated using pre-blast surveys and geotechnical monitoring. Following that review, it was determined that the damages claims were not the result of site activities,” the Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook.

Precision Blasting LLC, Maine Drilling & Blasting’s subsidiary in Georgia, did not respond to a request for comment.

Construction at the site continues, according to satellite images reviewed by Hunterbrook. 

Digital Realty has requested tax abatements of undisclosed size from the City of Forest Park Downtown Development Authority, Clayton County and Clayton County Public Schools, according to meeting minutes reviewed by Hunterbrook. In exchange, the company would sign a community benefits agreement worth about $5 million over 10 years including scholarships, park funding, and grants, based on Hunterbrook’s review of a draft agreement.

When asked about the community agreement, Digital Realty’s spokesperson told Hunterbrook: “Amounts remain subject to active negotiation and have not yet been finalized but are currently expected to exceed the $5 million initially requested.”

To date, the City of Forest Park has done little to address residents’ concerns about the project, according to Ann Pellegrine, another Forest Park resident who has sought answers from the city about the blasting and other environmental concerns.

Pellegrine said the project had remained secret under the city’s non-disclosure agreement with the developers until June 2025, when word leaked that the city’s design review board was examining plans for a data center — more than two months after the land sale had quietly closed in April 2025. At that point, it was too late for the residents to fight back, she said. “It didn’t have to go before council vote. It was completely done through the URA separately and in secret.” Georgia’s Urban Redevelopment law allows cities to grant the Urban Redevelopment Agency (URA) land-dealing powers, and once it does, the law allows the URA to do so without council vote.

URA chair James told Hunterbrook that URA entered into an NDA “in connection with the transaction” restricting the “URA from discussing the name of the company (Digital Realty).” Digital Realty denied signing an NDA with the city.

Pellegrine’s numerous efforts to obtain more information about the project through the Georgia Open Records Act have been “stonewalled,” she said, including, most recently with a $14,763 fee for the requested documents.

Zack Parker described a similar ordeal in an email to Hunterbrook. Since January, Parker has made nearly a dozen requests concerning the Fort Gillem redevelopment, blasting and incentives, including several for officials’ emails and texts, that he said “are simply being ignored.” The city’s own IT department had identified roughly 1,900 possible email matches concerning the redevelopment, he said, none of which he had received as of August. 

"I would bet everything I have that my requests are personally being delayed," Parker said.

The city of Forest Park did not respond to a request for comment. 

Pellegrine believes the “way these URAs have been set up and the way these corporations are coming in with their NDAs” are “exploiting communities like ours because we were weak.”

“We were naive and ignorant."

NEW: The Story Millrose Told Wall Street About Lennar Purchases Doesn’t Match The Evidence
items.u:
The Properties Tell a Different Story

Hunterbrook found approximately 95% of more than 1,000 identified Millrose home addresses listed for rent on Evergreen. 

Dozens of Millrose’s homes on Evergreen that Hunterbrook checked ranged from “available now” to a move-in date of October 21. Four out of five homes currently listed for rent had been purchased by Millrose over a month ago — in contrast to Millrose's description of the program as being tailored towards pre-sourced tenants.

Hunterbrook also called the number on the Evergreen listings to test what prospective tenants were being offered.

A reporter spoke with two Evergreen representatives about one Millrose-owned home currently advertised on its website. The representatives offered leases of 12 or 18 months and denied that there was any rent-to-own program available for the property. The house would not be available until October 16 at the earliest, they said, and that date could slip because construction or renovation work was still underway. Hunterbrook found terms on over 50 Evergreen ads offering 12 months minimum.

Hunterbrook reporters also called the sales offices at dozens of Lennar communities where Millrose purchased a home. None of those who answered said there was any rent-to-own program for buyers unable to qualify for a loan. One sales rep said they were just told that they might have such a program in mid-2027 but had no details to share. 

A listing or empty-looking house doesn’t necessarily mean no lease has been signed, and calls about one property don’t rule out a pilot program elsewhere. But if the rent-to-own homes described to Goldman exist, Hunterbrook could not find them. 

Lennar has its buyer. Millrose gets a new business with questionable economics

Millrose’s move into rentals was authorized through an August 27 amendment to the Founders’ Rights Agreement, subsequently filed with the SEC. It defined the new assets broadly as completed houses intended to operate as rentals. 

The benefits to Lennar are already visible. The 224 homes that have a listing history on realtor.com sat for a median of 86 days before Millrose’s deed was recorded. Millrose bought them at a slight discount from the last listing price — a median discount of about 4% — but still likely more than individual buyers who also got incentives averaging 13% of the purchase price. 

The benefits to Millrose — besides doing a solid for a homebuilder responsible for 72% of its second-quarter revenue — are less clear. And Hunterbrook’s analysis finds the company might actually be losing money on some of these purchases. 

Even assuming every house finds a tenant at the full advertised rental price, Hunterbrook’s estimated yield on the rentals based on specific state-level tax and average insurance rates — two of the most important expenses in a rental business — suggests Millrose will not make enough on most of their homes to clear its borrowing costs. 

Across the nearly 1,000 Millrose homes put up for rent, the gross rent comes to 8.44% of the price a year. But after factoring in taxes and insurance, proceeds to Millrose are more like 5.92%, below the 6.5% to 6.75% Millrose agreed to pay on its latest borrowing — the $1 billion of senior notes it sold on October 6, as disclosed to the SEC in an 8-K.

In states where Millrose invested most heavily — Florida and Texas — the economics are worse. In Florida, where insurance on a $300,000 house reportedly averages $8,471 a year, the yield is 4.9% before financing costs. South Carolina and Alabama, which have the lowest property taxes of any state where Millrose bought, according to Hunterbrook’s estimate, are the only ones that seem to exceed Millrose’s financing costs.

Millrose also told investors that the rentals' return will come partly from the eventual sale of the homes. “If the renter does not convert: Millrose sells the home on the open market. There is no put-back to the builder,” Goldman’s note says. 

But many of the homes sit in markets where prices are already falling and are projected to fall for at least another year. Typical home values in the zip codes where Millrose bought dropped 9% over the past year while the national index rose 1.3%, according to Zillow analytics. The decline is steepest where Millrose spent the most: Texas, which accounts for about 30% of the money, is down 4.2%.

Whether those homes can later be sold for more than Millrose paid in these markets is an open question.
